paragraphs: A big United Nations meeting about nature is happening in Yerevan, Armenia. Thousands of people are there, including groups from Ireland.
In 2022, countries promised to stop the loss of nature by 2030. But a new report says wild animal numbers fell by 73% in 50 years.
In Ireland, 90% of protected natural places are not healthy.
Christopher O'Sullivan is Ireland's Minister for Nature. He is at the meeting. He said Ireland is not on track to meet its goals. He wants to set up a special fund to pay for nature work.
Irish nature groups are worried. They say the EU plans to give less money to nature.
Ireland has called for more action to protect nature at a United Nations biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia. The meeting, called COP17, started on 19 October and ends this week.

Thousands of politicians, scientists and campaigners are checking progress on a promise made four years ago to stop and reverse the loss of nature by 2030. Before the summit, a report by the World Wildlife Fund found that wildlife populations had fallen by 73 per cent in 50 years.

In Ireland, a study last year found that 90 per cent of protected habitats were in poor health. Minister for Nature Christopher O'Sullivan, who is at the summit, said Ireland is "not on track" to reach its 2030 targets. He admitted that Ireland has not yet promised its own money, but said he is working to set up a special fund for nature restoration.
Irish wildlife groups at the meeting are worried about EU plans. They say funding for nature may be cut, and that some environmental rules could become weaker.
Ireland has urged greater efforts to protect nature at the UN Biodiversity Conference, known as COP17, which is taking place in Yerevan, Armenia, until the end of this week.

Delegates are reviewing progress on a 2022 commitment to halt and reverse the loss of nature by 2030. The outlook is bleak: a World Wildlife Fund report published just before the summit estimated that wildlife populations have declined by 73 per cent over 50 years.

Ireland's own record is poor. An assessment last year found that 90 per cent of protected habitats, and the species that depend on them, were in an unhealthy condition. Minister for Nature Christopher O'Sullivan acknowledged that the country is "not on track" to meet its 2030 targets and has yet to commit its own money, but said he is working on a dedicated nature restoration fund.

Irish environmental groups attending the talks say the EU's progress is not the full picture. They are concerned about proposed cuts to environmental funding in the next EU budget and plans to weaken some nature protection rules.
Ireland has called for a redoubling of efforts to safeguard the natural world at COP17, the UN biodiversity summit under way in Yerevan, Armenia.

Negotiators are taking stock of a pledge made in 2022 to halt and reverse nature loss by the end of the decade. The backdrop is sobering: a World Wildlife Fund report released on the eve of the summit put the decline in wildlife populations at 73 per cent over half a century.

Ireland is hardly in a position to lecture others. An assessment last year concluded that 90 per cent of protected habitats, together with the flora and fauna reliant on them, were in an unfavourable state. Minister for Nature Christopher O'Sullivan conceded that the country is "not on track" for its 2030 goals and has yet to pledge its own funds, though he said a dedicated restoration fund is in the pipeline.

Irish conservation groups at the talks warn that the EU's showcase legislation masks a less flattering reality, citing mooted cuts to environmental funding and proposals to dilute protections for birds and habitats.
Ireland has advocated more substantial efforts to protect biodiversity at COP17, the United Nations biodiversity conference currently being held in Yerevan, Armenia.

The conference is evaluating progress towards a 2022 commitment to halt and reverse the loss of nature by 2030. The evidence presented is far from encouraging: a report published by the World Wildlife Fund prior to the summit estimated that wildlife populations had declined by 73 per cent over a 50-year period.

Ireland's domestic performance is similarly concerning. An assessment conducted last year found that 90 per cent of protected habitats, and the species dependent upon them, were in poor condition. Consequently, the Minister for Nature, Christopher O'Sullivan, acknowledged that the country is "not on track" to achieve its 2030 targets. Although Ireland has not yet allocated national funding, he indicated that a dedicated nature restoration fund is being developed.

Nevertheless, Irish environmental organisations contend that the EU's legislative achievements present an incomplete picture. They have highlighted proposed reductions in environmental funding and a potential weakening of habitat protection requirements.
Ireland has urged greater efforts to protect nature at the UN Biodiversity Conference, known as COP17, which is taking place in Yerevan, Armenia, until the end of this week.

Delegates are reviewing progress on a 2022 commitment to halt and reverse the loss of nature by 2030. The outlook is bleak: a World Wildlife Fund report published just before the summit estimated that wildlife populations have declined by 73 per cent over 50 years.

Ireland's own record is poor. An assessment last year found that 90 per cent of protected habitats, and the species that depend on them, were in an unhealthy condition. Minister for Nature Christopher O'Sullivan acknowledged that the country is "not on track" to meet its 2030 targets and has yet to commit its own money, but said he is working on a dedicated nature restoration fund.

Irish environmental groups attending the talks say the EU's progress is not the full picture. They are concerned about proposed cuts to environmental funding in the next EU budget and plans to weaken some nature protection rules.
